prompt: Kátia asks Renata whether Matching may put a Redis cache in front of Tracking. Renata has an opinion in ten seconds. Why does she ask four questions instead of saying yes?
hint: Think about what happens next month, not today.

choices.text: Caches at Carreto need the architect's approval, one by one
choices.why: There is no such rule in the lesson. If there were one, it would be a standard, and Renata would say so plainly.

choices.text: A yes solves today's problem and brings the team back with the next one
choices.why: Right: answering every question makes the architect the queue each design waits in, and teaches the team nothing it keeps.

choices.text: She does not know Tracking well enough to give an opinion
choices.why: She has worked at Carreto for six years and knows Tracking; she had a view within ten seconds and chose not to lead with it.

choices.text: Questions protect her if the cache fails later on
choices.why: The lesson's reasons are about the team's knowledge and its ownership of the decision, not about who gets the blame.

prompt: Which of Renata's four questions led Matching to a fix it had not thought of, before any cache was added?
hint: One question took the favourite option off the table for a moment.

choices.text: What number are you trying to move, and by how much exactly?
choices.why: It turned "slow" into 1.8 s against a target of 400 ms, which is essential, but it did not uncover the wasted call.

choices.text: What happens when the cached position is wrong?
choices.why: It shaped the sixty-second expiry the team chose; it did not find the second call.

choices.text: Who else reads these positions?
choices.why: It exposed the risk of the map and the offer disagreeing, a different finding.

choices.text: What would you try first if a cache were not allowed?
choices.why: Right: a widening question. Looking again without the cache, the team found a call fetching a driver's whole history, and removing it took the 95th percentile from 1.8 s to 650 ms.

prompt: An architect asks a team: "Don't you think a queue would be better here?" What kind of question is this, by the lesson?
hint: Ask whether the speaker already holds an answer.

choices.text: A widening one, because it puts an alternative in front of the team
choices.why: A widening question asks the team for alternatives. This one supplies the alternative and asks the team to agree with it.

choices.text: A leading one: an answer in disguise
choices.why: Right: it is an instruction with a question mark, and it adds a guessing game. If the architect has a view, the honest move is to state it and say what kind of view it is.

choices.text: A probing one, since it tests the design against a different structure
choices.why: Probing questions ask what happens when something fails or grows. This one does not ask about the design's behaviour at all.

choices.text: A clarifying one, turning the request into a problem
choices.why: Clarifying questions ask for the goal and the number. This one skips straight to a solution.

prompt: Match each thing Renata says to the hat she is wearing.
hint: Ask who decides in each case.

pairs.left: "My advice is to measure before you cache. It is your call."
"Services read another team's data through its API. That is a standard."
pairs.right: pointing at a standard: already decided

pairs.left: "This changes the contract with Tracking, so Tracking's lead and I decide it."
pairs.right: making a decision: the architect with those affected

right_distractors: calling a vote: the forum decides by majority

prompt: At 02:10 a Payments deploy is failing and payouts are stuck. Bruno phones Renata to ask whether to roll back or push a fix forward. What fits the lesson?
hint: One of the situations where asking is the wrong help.

choices.text: Ask him what number he is trying to move, then what else he considered
choices.why: Those questions are for a design conversation. During an incident the team needs a decision in minutes.

choices.text: Remind him that under the advice process the decision is his team's, and wait
choices.why: The advice process says who decides; it does not tell an adviser to withhold a view when somebody asks for one in an emergency.

choices.text: Give her view at once, with a one-line reason, and leave the learning for the review
choices.why: Right: something is on fire, so she answers directly. A sentence of reasoning still lets Bruno reuse it, and the learning happens in the review afterwards.

choices.text: Raise it at the architecture forum so every team sees the decision
choices.why: The forum is where decisions become visible over weeks. Payouts are stuck now.

prompt: Lesson 3's process lets anyone make an architectural decision, after first asking the people it affects and people with expertise for their ___.
hint: What the person deciding is free not to follow.

prompt: What did Renata look for first in Ícaro's design document, before reading the solution?
hint: Without it, a review is a matter of taste.

choices.text: Clear names for the states and the queues
choices.why: Naming came last, as a nit. Starting there is the proofreading pass the lesson warns against.

choices.text: Whether the retry schedule matches what other teams use
choices.why: Consistency with other teams says nothing about whether this design meets its own measure.

choices.text: How the worker is deployed and monitored
choices.why: Operations matter, but they come after knowing what the design is for and how its success is measured.

choices.text: The problem, and the number that says whether it works
choices.why: Right: the document had the problem and lacked the measure. With the 24-hour promise written in, every later comment had something to be tested against.

prompt: Ícaro's design retries a failed payout after 5 minutes, then 15 more, then 60 more. How many minutes after the first failure is the last retry?
hint: Add the three delays.

prompt: In the failure walk, why was the bank's timeout the most dangerous case in Ícaro's design?
hint: What does a timeout tell the caller about the other side?

choices.text: A timeout hides whether the money moved, so a retry pays twice
choices.why: Right: a timeout means no answer arrived, not that nothing happened. The remedy is an idempotency key per payout and a status check before retrying.

choices.text: The bank charges Carreto a fee for every request that times out
choices.why: Nothing in the design or the lesson involves fees. The risk is a driver paid twice.

choices.text: Three timeouts in a row wake the on-call engineer at night
choices.why: An unnecessary alert is noise. A double payment is money that may not come back.

choices.text: The queue drops a message when the bank does not answer in time
choices.why: A lost message is a separate failure the walk also found; it leaves a payout stuck rather than paying it twice.

prompt: Which of these review comments on Ícaro's design deserves the label "blocking"?
hint: Blocking means unsafe, or missing the stated measure.

choices.text: I would call the state awaiting_retry rather than retrying
choices.why: A matter of wording, so a nit the author ignores freely.

choices.text: Have you thought about a different queue product?
choices.why: A suggestion at most: it is not blocking unless the queue fails a stated requirement.

choices.text: A retry after a timeout risks paying a driver twice
choices.why: Right: correctness is the attribute that matters most for payouts, and this breaks it. The design cannot go ahead until it is fixed.

choices.text: The state diagram for a payout is clear and complete
choices.why: Praise, and worth writing, but it asks the author for nothing.

prompt: Put the steps of Renata's design review in the lesson's order.
hint: From what the design is for, to what it does, to what you write.
items: Find the problem and the number that measures it
Name the quality attribute that matters most
Walk each box and arrow, asking how it fails
Write the comments, each with a label
trap: Starting with the comments turns the review into proofreading: names and wording get attention and the double payment does not.

prompt: Which of these habits make a design review more useful to a junior author? Choose all that apply.
hint: The lesson lists five habits; two of the options here reverse one of them.

choices.text: Writing "this retries a timeout" rather than "you forgot timeouts"
choices.why: Yes: review the design, not the author.

choices.text: Rewriting the weak section so the author sees how it should look
choices.why: It makes the design the reviewer's, and teaches the author that drafts get replaced.

choices.text: Saying in one line what is good about the design
choices.why: Yes: it tells the author what to keep doing.

choices.text: Marking a naming preference as blocking so it is not ignored
choices.why: Blocking is for unsafe designs or a missed measure. Inflating labels hides the one comment that matters.

choices.text: Moving to a whiteboard when serious comments pile up
choices.why: Yes: past a handful, thirty minutes in person beats a long thread.

prompt: Why did Renata stop writing Carreto's new ADRs herself after her first two months?
hint: What does writing one teach?

choices.text: Her records were too long for the teams to read
choices.why: The lesson says she wrote them quickly and well. Quality was not the problem.

choices.text: The advice process forbids the architect from writing records
choices.why: It does not; she still wrote 5 of the next 31. The point is who learns from writing them.

choices.text: Writing one is how developers learn design
choices.why: Right: writing a record is where a developer learns to state a context, name the options that lost and say what a decision costs. By writing all of them, Renata was keeping that practice for herself.

choices.text: Tomás asked her to spend that time writing code
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so. The change was hers, and the reason was what the writer learns.

prompt: When Renata pairs on a design, who holds the pen, and why?
hint: Watching teaches one thing and drawing teaches another.

choices.text: Renata, so the developer learns what a good diagram looks like
choices.why: That teaches recognition. The developer watches her think instead of thinking.

choices.text: Whoever knows the system best, so that the diagram on the board is accurate
choices.why: Accuracy of the drawing is not the goal of the session; the developer's reasoning is.

choices.text: The less experienced person, so Renata sees where their thinking stops
choices.why: Right: the developer does the thinking, and Renata learns exactly where to help, as with Diego's offline design.

choices.text: Each in turn, swapping every fifteen minutes
choices.why: A fair rule for pair programming, but the lesson's point is that the less experienced person draws and the architect asks.

prompt: Put the four steps for handing over a kind of decision in order, from the architect holding it to the developer holding it.
hint: The review moves from before the decision to after it.
items: You decide, and I review before it is final
You decide, and tell me afterwards
trap: Swapping the last two hides the real difference between them: whether the architect sees the decision before or after it takes effect.

prompt: Kátia is at step 4 for Matching's internal design and at step 2 for anything that changes a contract with Payments. What does that show?
hint: Where would a mistake land in each case?

choices.text: The step goes with the kind of decision, not the person
choices.why: Right: a mistake inside Matching stays in Matching; a mistake in a contract lands on another team, so it gets a closer look.

choices.text: Renata trusts Kátia less now than when she started in the role
choices.why: Kátia was at both steps from Renata's first week. Nothing moved backwards.

choices.text: Kátia is part-way through and will reach step 4 for both soon
choices.why: She may, but the lesson's point is that the two steps differ for a reason, not that one is behind.

choices.text: Contracts go to the forum instead
choices.why: The forum makes decisions visible; it does not take them away from the steps.

prompt: Renata's kata briefs describe a tool library and a school canteen, not freight. Why?
hint: What would a group lean on if the brief were about Carreto?

choices.text: Freight is too complex to design in forty-five minutes
choices.why: A brief is a few paragraphs in any domain; the reason is not size.

choices.text: So nobody leans on what they already know of Carreto's systems
choices.why: Right: in an unfamiliar business everybody has to reason from the brief, which is the practice the kata exists for.

choices.text: So the designs from the kata are reusable at other companies
choices.why: The designs are thrown away. The discussion of the trade-offs is the product.

choices.text: Real Carreto problems would expose confidential plans to juniors
choices.why: The participants already work at Carreto. Confidentiality is not the reason given.

prompt: In the ten months after the change, Carreto accepted 31 ADRs and Renata wrote 5 of them. What percentage was written by somebody else? Round to the nearest whole number.
hint: Subtract hers first, then divide by the total.

prompt: Diego asks Renata which version of the CT-e layout the tax authority will accept from next month. What should she do?
hint: Is this a judgement or a fact?

choices.text: Ask what he would try if he could not find out
choices.why: Asking works for judgements a team has to own. Turning a fact into a puzzle only wastes his time.

choices.text: Answer, or point to where it is written
choices.why: Right: it is a fact, not a judgement, which is the first of the four situations where she answers directly.

choices.text: Suggest he write an ADR about which layout version to use
choices.why: There is no decision to record; the tax authority made it.

choices.text: Raise it at the forum so every team hears the answer at once
choices.why: Overkill for a fact, and it delays a one-sentence answer by weeks.

prompt: A year on, fewer design questions reach Renata than in her first month. Which reading fits the lesson's measure?
hint: What is the measure the lesson names for all of this?

choices.text: Good, if sound decisions made without her held steady or grew
choices.why: Right: fewer questions is good news only alongside the decisions; the lesson measures how many sound decisions happen without the architect.

choices.text: Bad: an architect should be in more decisions over time
choices.why: That is the bottleneck of lesson 17. The goal is decisions made well without her.

choices.text: Good in any case, because her time is the scarcest in the company
choices.why: Fewer questions could also mean teams gave up asking and decide badly. The count alone does not say.

choices.text: Meaningless: questions reaching the architect say little about design
choices.why: It is one of the three columns Renata keeps, because questions a team could have answered alone are a signal.

prompt: Match each question to its kind.
hint: Goal, failure, alternatives, or an answer in disguise.

pairs.left: "What number are you trying to move?"
"What happens at ten times the load?"
"What would you do if this option were not allowed?"
"Don't you think a queue would be better here?"

prompt: Ícaro's alert fired after three failed retries. Which failure did that leave silent?
hint: A failure that produces no failed retry at all.

choices.text: A bank timeout on the first attempt
choices.why: A timeout is followed by retries, so if they keep failing, the alert fires.

choices.text: A worker crash after the table was updated
choices.why: If the table was already updated, the payout's state is correct; the dangerous crash is the one before the update.

choices.text: A driver whose bank account has been closed
choices.why: Each retry fails, so after three the alert fires and a person looks at it.

choices.text: A payout whose message was lost from the queue
choices.why: Right: a lost message is never retried, so it never fails three times, and the payout sits in retrying with nothing noticing. The fix was a nightly sweep.
